name: Under-eye cooling mask
lead: An under-eye cooling mask is a reusable gel or cold-pack patch worn over the lower eyelids and cheeks for a few minutes, typically after sleep or a late night, with the aim of reducing the look of puffy eyes. It is a form of local cryotherapy, the therapeutic use of low temperatures, which is more widely used for sprains, muscle soreness and swelling after surgery or soft tissue injury.[1]

The proposed mechanism is that cooling narrows blood vessels and reduces blood flow to swollen tissue.[1] No published trial appears to have tested cooling masks for everyday morning puffiness in otherwise healthy people. The closest evidence comes from surgical patients: a 2024 randomized trial after rhinoplasty found that a cooling gel eye mask was associated with lower pain and swelling scores than ice in a latex glove,[2] and a 2025 pilot study found that a cooled periocular mask reduced eyelid swelling for the first day or so after blepharoplasty.[3]
Cold exposure has documented limits and risks, including contraindications in people with cold allergy or cold-induced urticaria, and rare cold injury with prolonged or intense cooling.[1][4]

paras: Cooling eye masks are usually soft gel-filled pads, sometimes shaped to sit over the lower lids and upper cheeks, that are stored in a refrigerator or freezer and then worn while resting. Some are strap-on masks that cover the whole eye area. They are a commercial version of the long-standing practice of placing a cold compress or chilled objects on the eyes.

Cryotherapy lowers tissue temperature and narrows the blood vessels, which reduces blood flow to the cooled area. Reference summaries describe this vasoconstriction as the basis for using cold to limit swelling after injury or surgery.[1]

A small laboratory study in six healthy adults, in which a cryotherapy unit cooled the knee for an hour, found that skin blood flow fell sharply during cooling and remained reduced for two hours of rewarming, even though skin temperature had largely recovered. The authors described this as persistent vasoconstriction and suggested it might contribute to non-freezing cold injury in some settings.[4] That study did not examine the eyelids or cosmetic masks.
No published clinical trial has evaluated an under-eye cooling mask for ordinary morning puffiness or under-eye bags in the general population. Evidence from related settings is as follows.

A 2024 randomized clinical trial published in Plastic and Aesthetic Nursing compared ice placed in disposable latex gloves with a cooling gel eye mask in patients after rhinoplasty. Outcomes included eye bruising, periorbital and facial swelling, pain and comfort. On the first postoperative day the ice-glove group had higher scores for pain around the eyes, facial pain and periorbital edema, and higher facial edema scores in the first hour. Patients using the gel mask reported sleeping more comfortably. The authors concluded that cooling gel eye masks reduced pain and swelling after rhinoplasty.[2]

A prospective pilot study of 23 patients (46 eyes) used 3D photography to compare one eye treated with a cooled periocular mask (17 degrees C for one hour) with the untreated fellow eye after upper blepharoplasty. Treated eyes had a smaller increase in eyelid area immediately afterwards and at 24 hours, but the difference was no longer significant at two weeks. The study was small, single-centre and had no conventional cold-pack comparator.[3]

Wikipedia notes that ice-pack therapy is widely used and generally agreed to ease symptoms, but that testing has produced conflicting results about its effectiveness, and that some researchers have questioned whether icing after injury is helpful or may delay healing.[1] Systematic reviews of cryotherapy after knee replacement are described as inconclusive.[1] These findings concern injuries and surgery rather than cosmetic eye puffiness.

Contraindications listed for cryotherapy include cold allergy and conditions made worse by cold exposure such as urticaria and Raynaud syndrome, as well as impaired circulation or sensation in the treated area.[1] Frostbite and cold injury are associated with intense or prolonged cooling,[1][4] which is why products are usually designed for short applications at refrigerator rather than freezer-burn temperatures. The skin around the eyes is thin, and published surgical protocols use moderate temperatures; the pilot blepharoplasty study chose 17 degrees C because a 15 degrees C setting was poorly tolerated in preliminary testing.[3]

Puffiness has several possible causes, including fluid retention, allergy, fat prolapse and medical conditions, and a cooling mask is not designed to treat the underlying cause of persistent swelling. No trial has examined how long any cosmetic effect lasts.

Cooling masks and similar cold-compress routines are a common low-cost part of morning skincare and appear in appearance-focused discussions as a quick way to look less tired. The mechanism that proponents cite is vasoconstriction and reduced fluid pooling, in line with the physiology described in cryotherapy references.[1]

Products differ in whether they are gel pads or strap-on masks, whether they are intended for refrigerator or freezer storage, and in the thickness of the cloth barrier between gel and skin. Manufacturer instructions generally advise limiting application time and avoiding direct contact with frozen gel, and the cryotherapy literature lists cold allergy as a contraindication.[1]

timeline.event: Physician James Arnott is credited in some accounts with early therapeutic use of salt-and-ice mixtures for pain and inflammation.[1]
Laboratory study reports persistent reduction in skin blood flow after cutaneous cooling in healthy adults.[4]
Randomized trial reports a cooling gel eye mask was associated with less swelling and pain than ice gloves after rhinoplasty.[2]
Pilot study reports reduced eyelid swelling with a cooled periocular mask after blepharoplasty.[3]
